title: I'm a Microsoft veteran. Here's who I'd hire for the AI transition
excerpt: Rob Collie, a veteran Microsoft engineer, offers tips on how to successfully integrate AI into your business and who to hire for the transition.
content_html:
I'm a founder and decadelong Microsoft engineer. Here's who I'd hire to lead the next stage of AI.

By Katherine Li

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Rob Collie, a former Microsoft engineering leader. Collie's book about organizational AI strategy, "Fair Game," will be published on August 11. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I spent 13 years at Microsoft and was one of the founding engineers behind Power BI, a platform that helps clients visualize data and infuse insights into other Microsoft apps, before founding my own data and AI consulting firm.

Like a lot of business leaders, I spent the past couple of years trying to figure out what AI actually means for companies.

I came away with one big conclusion: Most companies are approaching AI the wrong way. The future isn't simply buying more AI-powered software or rushing to build your own large language model.

The real opportunity is teaching today's AI models how your business actually works — and empowering the right people inside your company to do it.

Off-the-shelf AI isn't enough

When I started figuring out our own AI strategy, I kept running into a disconnect. Everyone says AI will change everything, but when business leaders try to use it, they often struggle to make it useful.

The first wave of enterprise AI adoption assumed companies could simply buy AI-powered software and call it transformation. We're already seeing that it isn't delivering on the promise.

Businesses have to customize AI to fit the way they actually operate.

I think Satya Nadella is absolutely right when he talks about every company eventually building its own AI. He's talking about what I call the deep end of the pool: training or modifying your own large language models.

We'll probably get there eventually. But that's not where most organizations should begin.

The shallow end is far more practical. Today's LLMs are already incredibly capable if you treat them like a new employee instead of expecting them to automatically know your business. It's almost like they have PhDs in every possible human subject, but they would still be a new hire at your company.

They don't know your internal processes, your strategy, or your institutional knowledge.

Instead of building a new model, companies should build systems around existing models that feed them the right context at the right time. Think of commercial LLMs as Lego bricks. If you connect them to your company's data, workflows, and software, you can generate enormous returns without training your own model.

Master customization first. Then worry about building your own models.

The people I'd bet on are "crafters"

The biggest AI opportunity isn't necessarily hiring more AI researchers. It's finding the people already solving problems inside your business.

Software developers and data professionals will be incredibly valuable because connecting LLMs to business systems is fundamentally a software and data challenge. But there's another group I think leaders overlook.

In my upcoming book, I call them "crafters."

They're the people who build the spreadsheet everyone relies on. They automate tedious work. They create dashboards. They write scripts. They're embedded inside the business, solving problems that IT never had time to tackle.

My own research suggests that about 1 in 16 people fit this crafter profile. There are actually more crafters than professional software developers.

For years, they were limited by their technical skills. AI changes that. The crafters of the world can now write real software with the help of AI. That's why I think the combination of vibe coding and these business insiders is a secret weapon.

When I look for AI leaders, I wouldn't start by asking who knows the most about AI. I'd ask, "Who's the Excel guru? Who's the person everyone goes to when something breaks? Who keeps inventing clever solutions that make the business run?"

Those are the people already thinking like builders.

You can also find them by looking for the artifacts they've created — the spreadsheets, dashboards, automations, and tools that quietly keep critical business functions running.

I also don't think companies should wait for a top-down AI strategy before getting started.

Organizations run on thousands of individual workflows. No CEO can redesign all of them from headquarters.

The companies that succeed will start with small customization wins close to the business, learn from those successes, and expand from there.

和许多商业领袖一样，我在过去的几年里试图弄清楚人工智能对公司到底意味着什么。

我得出了一个重要结论：大多数公司都以错误的方式对待人工智能。 未来不仅仅是购买更多人工智能驱动的软件或急于构建自己的大型语言模型。

真正的机会是教导当今的人工智能模型您的业务如何实际运作，并授权公司内部合适的人员来做到这一点。

现成的人工智能还不够

当我开始制定我们自己的人工智能策略时，我总是陷入脱节。 每个人都说人工智能将改变一切，但当企业领导者尝试使用它时，他们往往很难让它发挥作用。

第一波企业人工智能采用假设公司可以简单地购买人工智能驱动的软件并称之为转型。 我们已经看到它没有兑现承诺。

企业必须定制人工智能以适应他们的实际运营方式。

我认为萨蒂亚·纳德拉（Satya Nadella）谈到每家公司最终都会构建自己的人工智能时绝对正确。 他正在谈论我所说的池的深处：训练或修改你自己的大型语言模型。

我们最终可能会到达那里。 但这不是大多数组织应该开始的地方。

浅端更加实用。 如果你像对待新员工一样对待今天的法学硕士，而不是期望他们自动了解你的业务，那么他们已经非常有能力了。 这几乎就像他们拥有所有可能的人类学科的博士学位，但他们仍然是你公司的新员工。

他们不了解你的内部流程、你的策略或你的机构知识。

公司不应该构建新模型，而应该围绕现有模型构建系统，在正确的时间为他们提供正确的环境。 将商业法学硕士视为乐高积木。 如果将它们连接到公司的数据、工作流程和软件，您无需训练自己的模型即可产生巨大的回报。

首先掌握定制。 然后担心构建自己的模型。

我打赌的人是“工匠”

最大的人工智能机会并不一定是雇佣更多的人工智能研究人员。 它正在寻找已经在解决您企业内部问题的人。

软件开发人员和数据专业人员将非常有价值，因为将法学硕士与业务系统连接起来从根本上来说是一个软件和数据挑战。 但我认为领导者忽视了另一个群体。

在我即将出版的书中，我称他们为“工匠”。

他们是构建每个人都依赖的电子表格的人。 他们将繁琐的工作自动化。 他们创建仪表板。 他们写剧本。 它们嵌入到业务中，解决 IT 从未有时间解决的问题。

我自己的研究表明，大约十六分之一的人符合这种工匠特征。 实际上，工匠的数量比专业软件开发人员的数量还要多。

多年来，他们一直受到技术技能的限制。 人工智能改变了这一点。 世界各地的工匠现在可以在人工智能的帮助下编写真正的软件。 这就是为什么我认为氛围编码和这些商业内部人士的结合是一个秘密武器。

当我寻找人工智能领导者时，我不会首先问谁最了解人工智能。 我会问：“Excel 大师是谁？ 当出现问题时，每个人都会去找谁？ 谁不断发明让企业运转的聪明解决方案？”

这些人已经像建设者一样思考。

您还可以通过查找他们创建的工件来找到它们 - 电子表格、仪表板、自动化和安静地保持关键业务功能运行的工具。

我也不认为公司应该等到自上而下的人工智能战略出台后再开始。

组织运行数千个单独的工作流程。 没有哪个首席执行官能够在总部重新设计所有这些。

成功的公司将从靠近业务的小型定制胜利开始，从这些成功中学习，并以此为基础进行扩展。
